extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and deductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the principal kinds of propositions (simple identities, partial identities, limited identities, negative propositions) and the common forms of deductive inference (immediate inference, substitution, inference from two identities, etc.). Emphasizes reducing propositions to identities and rules for valid substitution and conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple identities (A = B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that assert the identity of single qualities, causes of sensation, or groups of qualities; expressed in the form A = B (e.g., 'Colour of Pacific Ocean = Colour of Atlantic Ocean'; definitions such as 'Common salt = Sodium chloride').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identity-form expressions for single qualities, groups of qualities, and definitions. Many mathematical and scientific theorems and definitions naturally take this form; treating propositions as identities simplifies inference and enables reciprocal statements (A = B implies B = A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as identities
rubrics_metrics.description: All definitions are necessarily of the identity form (e.g., 'Square = Equal-sided rectangle'; 'Chlorophyl = Green colouring matter of leaves').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term and its definition are given together, treat them as equivalent identities so either expression may be substituted for the other in inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial identities (universal affirmative as identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions like 'All mammalia are vertebrata' are partial identities: the class A is identical with a part of class B. Represented in this system as A = AB (the class A is identical with the class AB, a part of B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague indeterminate words like 'some' (A = VB). Prefer expressing universals by identity with an explicitly limited class (A = AB). This yields clearer substitution rules and reduces indeterminacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited identities (AB = AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of the form AB = AC express identity limited to the sphere A: 'Within the sphere of the class A, all the B's are all the C's.' Nothing is asserted about things outside A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about implied limitations or tacit conditions (the 'sphere' of discourse). Recognize that many scientific and legal statements are true only within an implied universe of discourse; these tacit limitations are part of practical argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative propositions and representation of difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative propositions express difference but always imply an agreement with other objects (every negative term has a corresponding positive complement). Differences can be represented by identities with negative terms (e.g., Quicksilver = Quicksilver not-solid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer representing judgments in forms that make implied agreements explicit. Difference by itself is 'incapable of becoming the ground of inference'; use the implied agreements (identities) to perform deductive reasoning. Be aware of the Law of Duality (positive term and its negative divide the universe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion and reciprocity of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity is essentially reciprocal: if A = B then B = A. Thus traditional conversion rules become unnecessary because any identity can be written in either order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When propositions are reduced to identities, conversion is trivial — write the identity in either order as needed. This removes the need for special rules or mnemonic conversion procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold interpretation: extension vs intension
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms and propositions may be read either in extension (quantitative, membership of individuals) or in intension (qualitative, the set of qualities denoted). Example: 'Exogens = Dicotyledons' may mean either the qualities coincide or every individual under one name falls under the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the intensive/qualitative form as primary because extensive meanings (classes) change over time while intensive meanings remain more stable. Be explicit which interpretation is intended since it affects inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate inference (adding same qualifier to identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: From A = B one may immediately infer AC = BC by joining an adjective or qualifying clause of the same nature to both sides of an identity (example: from 'Conductors of electricity = Non-electrics' infer 'Liquid conductors of electricity = Liquid non-electrics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is substitution applied to an identity; verify by the Law of Thought (AC = AC and substitute B for A). This form of immediate inference is reliable and less error-prone than other immediate-inference methods (criticized: 'Immediate Inference by added Determinants').

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from two simple identities (transitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given B = A and B = C (or A = B and B = C), infer A = C: 'terms identical with the same term are identical with each other' (analogy to Euclid's axiom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitution: consider one identity as asserting a truth about B and the other as identifying B with A, then substitute to transfer the truth. This is a common and fundamental valid form of deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from a simple identity and a partial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A = B and B = BC (partial identity), substitution yields A = BC and possibly A = AC (by substituting definition of B), allowing transfer of attributes from the defined term to the defined class (e.g., 'Mont Blanc is highest mountain' and 'Mont Blanc is deeply covered with snow' gives 'The highest mountain in Europe is deeply covered with snow').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute definitions for terms or vice versa to propagate predicates; this is how definitions are used to shorten descriptive phrases and enable inference in scientific exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of inference from differences (no inference from two differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two propositions are both differences (A ≠ B and B ≠ C), no valid inference about A and C can be drawn in general. If one proposition is an identity and the other a difference, one may infer a difference (A = B and B ≠ C implies A ≠ C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on identities for deductive inference; recognize that difference alone generally does not permit inference about relations between the differing terms, so avoid attempting transitive conclusions from mere differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of universals without indeterminate terms ('some')
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of using an indeterminate adjective like 'some' (A = VB) to express 'All A's are some B's', prefer definite representations such as A = AB which assert identity of A with the class AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indeterminate symbols introduce complexity and prevent later replacement by special descriptions. Use more definite expressions when possible to maintain clarity and allow precise substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of tacit knowledge and implicit universes of discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Many propositions are expressed with implied tacit conditions (e.g., 'Large plants are plants devoid of locomotive power' or legal statements 'under the English law'). These tacit limitations form part of the working universe in which arguments operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make tacit conditions explicit when necessary, because the truth of many limited identities depends on the implied universe; awareness of the implicit sphere avoids misapplication of general statements.
